analysis.title: $100 Oil Is Pricing Fear — The Options Market Isn't
key_insights: Brent near $100 is explained by risk premium, not the current physical balance. Gulf exports have normalized, visible inventories remain above early-2025 levels, and GS sees September roughly balanced.
GS estimates roughly $20-25/bbl of risk premium remains embedded in crude.
The physical shortage has eased, but the buffer is thinner. Ex-OECD commercial inventories are around record lows and the availability of spare capacity is less certain.

The tail risk is another attack that takes Gulf flows back below 50% with a much thinner inventory cushion. GS argues stocks remain comfortably above operational minimums, but the system has less room to absorb another major disruption.

OVX is trading around the same level as when oil was below $80, even with crude near $100 after the surge since July. This differs from February/March, when rising oil came with a sharp repricing of oil volatility.
Call skew has moved back toward pre-war levels, and the options bid has been concentrated in puts.
Macro funds vulnerable to another oil spike have been buying outright delta rather than upside calls.
Flat price is pricing geopolitical fear while upside vol is not. The note argues one of them eventually has to move.

Pre-war versus current call skew in oil options: call skew has returned toward pre-war levels.

tension_points.bull_case: Flat price near $100 Brent reflects a geopolitical risk premium of $20-25/bbl and thinner buffers, with ex-OECD commercial inventories near record lows and less certain spare capacity.
tension_points.bear_case: Oil vol and call skew have not followed flat price higher. OVX is at the level seen when oil was below $80, call skew is back toward pre-war levels, and the options bid is in puts, so options are not pricing the same fear as flat price.
